newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - British minorities vote Labour,but for how long?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - British minorities vote Labour,but for how long?.

text.p: Britain's ethnic minorities traditionally vote overwhelmingly for the Labour Party, but rising living standards and disaffection among young blacks and Asians mean Labour can no longer take their support for granted.
Prime Minister John Major's Conservatives have been wooing the Asian electorate assiduously, claiming a common devotion to wealth creation and family values, and the effort may be paying dividends.

"Asians in Britain are beginning to question the traditional family vote, and party allegiance, far from being inherited, is giving way to a more demanding electorate," said Simon Braunholtz, director of political research at MORI.

According to a recent MORI poll, 86 percent of all blacks will vote for Labour. Support from the Asian community stands at 70 percent. Those votes could be crucial as Labour bids to end 18 years of Conservative rule.

It is estimated that although the Asian community makes up just three percent of the electorate, their votes could swing the result in 40 marginal constituencies. About six percent of Britain's total 59 million population are of ethnic origin.

The Conservatives are fielding eight Asian candidates this year against Labour's nine. Major's party has one Asian member of parliament to Labour's two and is busy trying to remove the stain caused by Enoch Powell 30 years ago.
A former Conservative minister, Powell's infamous "rivers of blood" speech in the 1960s, warning of the social dangers of unchecked immigration, remains a vivid memory for non-whites.
PRAISE FOR ASIAN ACHIEVEMENTS
In February, Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine spoke at a dinner to celebrate the richest 100 Asians in Britain.
He was unstinting in his praise for their achievements, "the equal of anything the indigenous population could parade".
The evening was hosted by Eastern Eye, a paper for the Asian community in Britain whose editorial line leans towards Labour, which has a large lead in opinion polls.
The edition circulated that evening published a letter taking the paper to task for its politics.

"I agree with the Prime Minister that the natural home of Asians is with the Conservative Party," said Jai Patel. "The tax burden that the Labour Party is sure to levy on small businesses will cripple them, and many of these are run by Asians."
In January, Major visited the Indian sub-continent with a large British press corps in tow.

It was easy to dismiss that trip as a glorified photo opportunity, aimed at the Asian vote back home, but cynics had to swallow their words later that month when Major made a plea for racial harmony at the Commonwealth Institute in London.
"I believe quite simply in the brotherhood of man -- men of all races, of all colours, of all creeds," Major said in a speech warmly welcomed by Britons of all creeds.

Shamit Saggar, politics lecturer at Queen Mary and Westfield College in London, said that if Major succeeded in laying the ghost of Powellism, the ethnic minorities, and Indians in particular, could begin to spread their vote more evenly.
"In 10 to 15 years time maybe, you would expect to see a significant minority of Asians voting for the Conservative Party, naturally, and in a sustained way from one election to another," he said.
MORE ASIANS MAY VOTE CONSERVATIVE -- BUT NOT YET
But the Conservative pitch for the Asian vote has had a limited immediate effect according to data collected by MORI in February for a popular Asian television channel, Zee TV.

Seventy percent of south Asians -- voters with Indian, Pakistani and Bangladeshi roots -- said they would vote Labour, up from the 64 percent that did so in the 1992 election, while the Conservative vote was likely to drop to 25 from 31 percent.
Saggar doubts the Conservatives, in power since 1979, will make an inroad into the Asian vote, this year at least.
"Would-be Asian Tories are stopping short of voting Tory. They're voting Labour by default," Saggar said.
BLACK VOTING

Among black people, there is strong resistance to voting at all. One poll on black voting intentions found that only 16 percent of black 18-to-24-year-olds were certain they would vote in the May 1 election. "Young, black would-be voters are holding back. They don't see politics as being particularly relevant to their needs," said Saggar.
Concerned at the apathy, campaigners have launched Operation Black Vote, which is targeting 50 key marginal seats and aims to bring ethnic minority issues more squarely on to the agenda.
MORI polls show that Labour is supported by around 85 percent of African, Black Caribbean and Black British voters.
But neither Major nor Labour leader Tony Blair were seen as particularly committed to the black population, and "force of habit" was cited as the main motivation for voting Labour.
"Just nine percent of Labour supporters spontaneously say they do so because they see it as a party for black people," MORI commented.
Bill Morris, black leader of the big Transport and General Workers Union, blamed the Labour leadership in a sharp attack in a letter to the Guardian newspaper.
"The revisionist tendency" in the party had concluded "there were no votes in anti-racism", he wrote, and was shunning the black community so as not to alienate the white middle class.
"Where black people have shown any sign of seeking selection in winnable seats, Labour headquarters has acted to close down the local parties and suspend the democratic process."
Labour's three black members of parliament are standing again, but it has only one new black candidate, adopted at the last minute in a poor, multi-racial east London constituency.
The Conservatives have no black MPs and no black candidates after the only one selected withdrew due to business commitments in late March.
